items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a climate with high temperatures (about 26-28 °C) all year, a small annual range and heavy rainfall in every month, typically over 2000 mm a year”.
items.answer: Humid tropical (equatorial) climate
items.markingKey: Humid tropical (equatorial) climate: a climate with high temperatures (about 26-28 °C) all year, a small annual range and heavy rainfall in every month, typically over 2000 mm a year. [1]

items.stem: Describe the characteristics of the humid tropical climate.
items.answer: Mean monthly temperatures about 26-28 °C with an annual range under 3 °C; high humidity; annual rainfall 1500-3000 mm, falling in all months, often in afternoon convectional storms; no distinct dry season (or a short one).
items.markingKey: 1 mark per characteristic with data [4]

items.stem: Compare the climate of a seasonally humid tropical area with that of a humid tropical area.
items.answer: Both are hot all year; seasonally humid areas have a larger annual temperature range, lower annual rainfall concentrated in a wet season, and a dry season of several months with low humidity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed comparison [3]

items.stem: “The difference between humid tropical and seasonally humid tropical climates is mainly a difference of rainfall rather than temperature.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to dry season, the ITCZ and Köppen classification.
items.answer: For: Rainfall total and seasonality define the contrast: rain in all months near the equator versus a long dry season further away; temperatures are hot all year in both. Against: Seasonally humid areas have larger annual and diurnal temperature ranges, higher maxima before the rains and cooler dry-season nights; humidity and evapotranspiration differ. Conclusion: Rainfall regime is the defining difference, though temperature range differences are significant and linked to it.

items.stem: A student writes: “Equatorial climates are the hottest climates in the world.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Hot deserts have higher maximum temperatures because skies are clear; cloud keeps equatorial maxima around 30-32 °C.

items.stem: Explain why temperatures in the humid tropics vary little through the year.
items.answer: The sun is high in the sky all year and day length is about 12 hours, so insolation is consistently high; cloud cover limits extremes.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, a belt of low pressure where the north-east and south-east trade winds converge”.

items.markingKey: ITCZ: the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, a belt of low pressure where the north-east and south-east trade winds converge. [1]

items.stem: Explain how the Hadley cell produces both humid and arid tropical climates.
items.answer: At the ITCZ, intense heating and convergence cause air to rise, cool and condense, giving heavy rain; the air flows polewards aloft, cools, and sinks at about 30°, warming adiabatically and creating dry subtropical highs; trade winds return air to the ITCZ.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [4]

items.stem: Explain the seasonal migration of the ITCZ and its effect on rainfall.
items.answer: The ITCZ follows the zone of maximum heating (overhead sun) north in June-July and south in December-January, bringing a wet season to the areas it passes over; places it does not reach remain dry.

items.stem: Fig. 1.2 shows that the ITCZ migrates between about 5°S in January and 20°N in July over Africa. A student estimates that a station at 18°S lies within the rainy zone of the ITCZ for about 3 months of the year. Explain why places near the equator may have two rainfall maxima.
items.answer: The ITCZ passes overhead twice a year, around the equinoxes, as it moves north and then south.

items.answer: (a) 9 months (b) June-September (c) The ITCZ spends less time over places nearer its limits; for the rest of the year they are under the influence of the subtropical high and dry trade winds.

items.stem: “The movement of the ITCZ is the main factor explaining the climates of the tropics.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to the Hadley cell and monsoons.
items.answer: For: The ITCZ brings convergence and convectional rain, controlling the timing and length of wet seasons from equatorial to savanna climates. Against: Subtropical highs, cold ocean currents, relief and rain shadows, monsoon pressure systems and ENSO also shape tropical climates; local factors create variation (e.g. the dry coast of Peru). Conclusion: The ITCZ is the main control over rainfall seasonality, but other circulation features and local factors are needed for a full explanation.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “ITCZ”?

The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, a belt of low pressure where the north-east and south-east trade winds converge.
Belts of sinking, warming, dry air at about 25-35° N and S, associated with deserts.
The low-latitude circulation cell with rising air at the ITCZ, poleward flow aloft, sinking air at the subtropical highs and surface trade winds.

items.stem: Explain how El Niño affects tropical climates.
items.answer: Weakened trade winds allow warm water to spread east; convection shifts to the central and eastern Pacific; drought in Indonesia, Australia and southern Africa; floods in Peru and Ecuador; weaker Indian monsoon.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an intense low-pressure system that forms over warm tropical oceans, with sustained winds of at least 119 km/h; called a hurricane or typhoon in some regions”.
items.answer: Tropical cyclone
items.markingKey: Tropical cyclone: an intense low-pressure system that forms over warm tropical oceans, with sustained winds of at least 119 km/h; called a hurricane or typhoon in some regions. [1]

items.stem: Explain the conditions needed for tropical cyclones to form.
items.answer: Sea surface at least 26-27 °C to a depth of about 60 m; latitude 5-20° so the Coriolis effect is strong enough; low vertical wind shear; moist, unstable air; an initial disturbance such as an easterly wave; upper-level divergence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per condition [4]

items.stem: Explain why tropical cyclones weaken when they move over land.
items.answer: They lose their supply of warm, moist air and latent heat; friction over land reduces wind speed.

(b) Explain why the storm weakened after landfall.
items.answer: (a) day 1: below hurricane strength; day 2: category 1; day 3: category 5; day 4: category 1; day 5 (after landfall): below hurricane strength (b) Loss of warm, moist air and latent heat energy; increased surface friction.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that tropical cyclones bring more benefits than problems to tropical environments? In your answer you may refer to ecosystems and vulnerability.
items.answer: For: They supply rainfall that recharges water stores and reservoirs, break droughts and redistribute heat. Against: They cause storm surges, flooding, landslides and destruction of crops and buildings (Cyclone Idai 2019, Typhoon Haiyan 2013); deaths and long recovery. Conclusion: Physical benefits exist, but for people the damage usually outweighs them, especially in vulnerable low-income countries.

items.stem: Explain the contribution of tropical cyclones to rainfall in tropical climates.
items.answer: They bring very heavy rain over a few days (often hundreds of mm), contributing a large share of annual rainfall in places such as the Philippines and north-west Australia, but also floods and landslides.

(b) Explain why storm surge often causes more deaths than wind.
items.answer: (a) Loss of warm, moist air and latent heat energy; increased surface friction. (b) Low pressure and strong onshore winds raise sea level several metres, flooding low-lying coasts and deltas quickly, e.g. Nargis in the Irrawaddy delta.

items.stem: “The movement of the ITCZ is the main factor explaining the climates of the tropics.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to monsoons, the Hadley cell and ENSO.
items.answer: For: The ITCZ brings convergence and convectional rain, controlling the timing and length of wet seasons from equatorial to savanna climates. Against: Subtropical highs, cold ocean currents, relief and rain shadows, monsoon pressure systems and ENSO also shape tropical climates; local factors create variation (e.g. the dry coast of Peru). Conclusion: The ITCZ is the main control over rainfall seasonality, but other circulation features and local factors are needed for a full explanation.

items.stem: “Tropical cyclones bring more benefits than problems to tropical environments.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: They supply rainfall that recharges water stores and reservoirs, break droughts and redistribute heat. Against: They cause storm surges, flooding, landslides and destruction of crops and buildings (Cyclone Idai 2019, Typhoon Haiyan 2013); deaths and long recovery. Conclusion: Physical benefits exist, but for people the damage usually outweighs them, especially in vulnerable low-income countries.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe the characteristics of the humid tropical climate. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “The length of the dry season increases with distance from the equator in the tropics.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Mean monthly temperatures about 26-28 °C with an annual range under 3 °C; high humidity; annual rainfall 1500-3000 mm, falling in all months, often in afternoon convectional storms; no distinct dry season (or a short one). (b) Correct. Further from the equator the ITCZ is overhead for a shorter period.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Compare the climate of a seasonally humid tropical area with that of a humid tropical area. (b) A student writes: “Equatorial climates are the hottest climates in the world.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Both are hot all year; seasonally humid areas have a larger annual temperature range, lower annual rainfall concentrated in a wet season, and a dry season of several months with low humidity. (b) Not correct. Hot deserts have higher maximum temperatures because skies are clear; cloud keeps equatorial maxima around 30-32 °C.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the difference between humid tropical and seasonally humid tropical climates is mainly a difference of rainfall rather than temperature? In your answer you may refer to Köppen classification, the ITCZ and dry season.
items.answer: For: Rainfall total and seasonality define the contrast: rain in all months near the equator versus a long dry season further away; temperatures are hot all year in both. Against: Seasonally humid areas have larger annual and diurnal temperature ranges, higher maxima before the rains and cooler dry-season nights; humidity and evapotranspiration differ. Conclusion: Rainfall regime is the defining difference, though temperature range differences are significant and linked to it.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the seasonal migration of the ITCZ and its effect on rainfall. (b) Explain how the Hadley cell produces both humid and arid tropical climates.
items.answer: (a) The ITCZ follows the zone of maximum heating (overhead sun) north in June-July and south in December-January, bringing a wet season to the areas it passes over; places it does not reach remain dry. (b) At the ITCZ, intense heating and convergence cause air to rise, cool and condense, giving heavy rain; the air flows polewards aloft, cools, and sinks at about 30°, warming adiabatically and creating dry subtropical highs; trade winds return air to the ITCZ.

items.answer: (a) The ITCZ follows the zone of maximum heating (overhead sun) north in June-July and south in December-January, bringing a wet season to the areas it passes over; places it does not reach remain dry. (b) Not correct. It lags the sun by a few weeks and migrates further over land than over the oceans.
